name: Australia
summary: A federation formed in 1901 from six British colonies on the continent of Australia, where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived for at least 50,000 years.

knownFor.label: Sydney Opera House
knownFor.note: Designed by Jørn Utzon; a World Heritage Site.

knownFor.label: Secret ballot
knownFor.note: Developed in the Australian colonies and often called the “Australian ballot”.

knownFor.label: ANZAC
knownFor.note: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, remembered on Anzac Day.

location.value: The continent of Australia, Tasmania and nearby islands; about 7.7 million km².

terrain.value: A dry interior (the Outback) with deserts; the Great Dividing Range along the east coast; the Great Barrier Reef.

climate.value: Mostly arid or semi-arid; tropical in the north; temperate in the south-east and south-west.

resources.value: Iron ore, coal, gold, natural gas, wool, wheat and beef.

disasters.value: Bushfires (Black Saturday 2009; the 2019–20 fires), droughts, floods and cyclones.

population.value: About 3.8 million in 1901; about 27 million today.

urbanisation.value: One of the most urbanised countries; most people live in coastal cities such as Sydney and Melbourne.

disease.value: The 1918–19 influenza; strict quarantine laws; a public health system (Medicare, 1984).

migration.value: British and Irish settlers, then post-war European migrants; Asian immigration since the end of the White Australia policy (1966–73).

economicBase.value: Wool and gold at first; today mining, farming exports, education and services.

tradeRoutes.value: Shipping to Britain at first; today mostly trade with China, Japan and the rest of Asia.

wealth.value: One of the world’s richest countries per person; long periods of growth.

moneyAndTax.value: The pound until 1966, then the Australian dollar; income tax and a goods and services tax (2000).

inequality.value: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples were excluded from many rights; the Stolen Generations of removed children.

governmentType.value: A federal parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy.

keyRulers.value: Edmund Barton (first prime minister, 1901). John Curtin. Robert Menzies. Gough Whitlam. Bob Hawke. John Howard. Anthony Albanese.

succession.value: Elections with compulsory voting (since 1924); the leader of the majority in the House of Representatives becomes prime minister.

institutions.value: Federal Parliament, the High Court, six states and two main territories.

stability.value: Very stable; the dismissal of Whitlam’s government in 1975 caused a constitutional crisis.

eliteConflict.value: Tensions between federal and state governments.

armyAndTech.value: Small professional forces; large volunteer armies in the World Wars.

majorWars.value: First World War (Gallipoli, 1915), Second World War, Korea, Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan.

territoryChange.value: Took over Papua (1906) and German New Guinea (1920 mandate) until Papua New Guinea’s independence in 1975.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to Britain, then to the United States (ANZUS treaty, 1951).

inventions.value: The black box flight recorder, Wi-Fi research (CSIRO), the cochlear implant.

scienceEducation.value: Public universities and schools; strong research in medicine and science.

openness.value: Restricted Asian immigration (White Australia policy) until the 1970s; now very multicultural.

religion.value: Mostly Christian historically; now the largest group says it has no religion.

languageWriting.value: English; more than 100 Aboriginal languages survive, many endangered.

artsArchitecture.value: Aboriginal art (including dot painting), the Sydney Opera House, film and literature.

socialStructure.value: Egalitarian ideals (“a fair go”); Aboriginal people gained the vote nationally in 1962 and the 1967 referendum counted them in the census.

sharedIdentity.value: National identity often linked to the ANZAC story, sport and the outdoors; reconciliation with First Nations is ongoing.

neighbours.value: Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and New Zealand across the sea.

ideasReligions.value: British law and parliamentary traditions; later Asian influences.

colonisation.value: British colonisation from 1788 took Aboriginal land without treaties; the High Court recognised native title in 1992 (Mabo).

riseSignals.value: The colonies federated in 1901 for common defence, trade and immigration control.

peakPeriod.value: Long post-war boom; decades of growth without recession (1991–2020).

declineSignals.value: Droughts and climate risks; debates about reconciliation.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Australia; Wikipedia: History of Australia (1901–1945) and (since 1945); ABS census.
